planting.note: Direct-sow in spring into dry, sandy, infertile soil in full sun, mimicking native sandhill and pine-scrub-oak habitat.

directions: Native to sandhills, flatwoods, and pine-scrub oak ridges from the Carolinas through Alabama and the Florida panhandle, this slender milkweed complements the already-present sandhill and tomentose milkweeds for well-drained zone 9 sites. It carries narrow, grayish leaves and small pink flower clusters in late spring, and like its sandy-habitat relatives it resents rich, moisture-retentive soil. Give it a lean, open spot in full sun rather than a mixed perennial border.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Fall-sow (dormant seeding is typical for coastal-prairie milkweeds) into lean, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: A true Texas Gulf Coast specialist, endemic to the coastal plain and coastal-prairie-to-salt-marsh transition from the coast north to Dallas County, this fine, narrow-leaved milkweed hosts both monarch and queen butterflies. It wants lean, well-drained coastal-prairie soil in full sun and resents being crowded by taller, lusher perennials. Establish it in an open prairie-style planting rather than a conventional mixed bed.

planting.note: Direct-sow in spring into caliche, calcareous, or sandy-loam soil in full sun; low, spreading habit suits a rock garden edge or lean prairie planting rather than a border.

directions: A low, spreading South Texas and western Edwards Plateau grassland species found in caliche, calcareous, and sandy-loam soils, this milkweed's near-prostrate habit makes it a distinct low-stature form valuable for dry, lean, limestone-based sites where taller milkweeds would look out of scale. It supports the same monarch and native-bee value as its taller relatives in a much smaller footprint, good for a rock garden or gravel bed edge. Give it sharp drainage and minimal supplemental water once established.
sources: Xerces Society - Milkweeds of Oklahoma and Texas
Texas Parks and Wildlife - Identification of Milkweeds in Texas

planting.note: Direct-sow in spring into clay or silty soil in filtered sun or part shade, matching its native desert-canyon riparian habitat rather than open full sun.

directions: A low-desert and riparian-canyon milkweed of the Arizona-New Mexico borderlands, growing naturally in filtered shade along clay and silty streambanks rather than open desert flats, making it a useful part-shade milkweed option distinct from the mostly full-sun species already in the collection. It serves as a documented monarch host in its native range and is sold through specialty desert-Southwest native nurseries. Give it clay or silty soil with some canopy protection rather than baking full sun.
sources: Xerces Society and NRCS - Pollinator Plants of the Desert Southwest: Native Milkweeds

planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings and plant in spring into consistently moist to wet soil at a pond margin or rain garden in full sun to part shade.

directions: Occurring in the US only along the Rio Grande in the southernmost tip of Texas and extending through Mexico into Central America, this heat-tolerant buttonbush is an excellent nectar source and companion to the already-present common buttonbush for deep South Texas pond margins and rain gardens. It grows considerably larger than its northern relative, eventually reaching tree-like proportions, so give it room along a wet bank rather than a small residential water feature. It tolerates standing water for extended periods but also handles seasonal dry-down once established.
